q: Which of the following is a freehold estate?
options: Life estate
Estate for years
Periodic tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) are ownership interests of indefinite duration. Estates for years, periodic tenancies, tenancies at will, and tenancies at sufferance are leasehold (less-than-freehold) estates.

q: A deed conveys land "to the Town of Clifton so long as the land is used as a public park." If the town stops using it as a park, what happens?
options: The grantor must first sue to exercise a right of re-entry
The town keeps title, because use conditions in deeds are void
Title automatically returns to the grantor (possibility of reverter)
The town's interest converts into a leasehold held from the grantor
explanation: Words of duration such as "so long as" or "while" create a fee simple determinable, which ends automatically when the condition is broken. A fee on condition subsequent ("but if") requires the grantor to act.

q: A deed conveys a lot to a buyer "but if alcohol is ever sold on the premises, the grantor may re-enter and reclaim the property." Alcohol is later sold. What is the result?
options: Title reverts to the grantor automatically on the sale
The buyer keeps title until the grantor acts to reclaim it
The deed is void from the date it was delivered
The buyer's estate becomes a leasehold estate
explanation: "But if" or "provided that" language creates a fee simple on condition subsequent. Breach gives the grantor a right of re-entry (reacquisition), but the estate does not end until the grantor exercises it.

q: An owner deeds a house "to Beth for life, then to Carlos." What interest does Carlos hold while Beth is alive?
options: A reversion
A life estate pur autre vie
A leasehold estate
A remainder
explanation: A future interest held by a third party who takes when the life estate ends is a remainder (Carlos is the remainderman). If the property were to return to the original grantor instead, the grantor's interest would be a reversion.

q: An owner deeds land "to Dana for the life of Eli." Dana dies while Eli is still living. What happens to the estate?
options: It passes to Dana's heirs or devisees until Eli dies
It ends immediately at Dana's death, since Dana was the holder
It reverts to the grantor at the moment of Dana's death
It becomes a fee simple absolute owned by Dana's heirs
explanation: A life estate pur autre vie is measured by the life of someone other than the holder (here Eli). It continues for Eli's lifetime, so it passes to Dana's estate if Dana dies first.

q: A residential tenant's one-year lease expired, and the tenant remains in possession without the landlord's consent. This tenant has a:
options: Tenancy at will
Periodic (month-to-month) tenancy
Tenancy at sufferance
Estate for years
explanation: A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover after a lawful tenancy ends, without the landlord's consent; it is not a new agreed lease. A tenancy at will exists with the landlord's permission. Self-help eviction is still prohibited.

q: Which of the following is a general lien?
options: A mortgage
A docketed money judgment
A mechanic's lien
A real property tax lien
explanation: A general lien attaches to all of the debtor's property within its reach, such as a judgment lien on all real property in the county. Mortgages, mechanic's liens, and property tax liens are specific liens on one parcel.

q: A creditor wins a money judgment and dockets it with the clerk of the county where the debtor owns two houses. What is the effect?
options: It is a lien only on the specific property named in the lawsuit
It is a lien on the debtor's personal property, but not on real estate
It attaches to a house only when the debtor later tries to sell it
It is a lien on his real property in that county, generally for 10 years
explanation: A docketed judgment is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, generally for 10 years. It is involuntary and is not limited to a single parcel.

q: A property has a mortgage recorded in 2019, a judgment lien docketed in 2021, and unpaid 2026 real property taxes. Which lien generally has first priority?
options: The real property tax lien
The mortgage, because it was recorded first
The judgment lien, because it is a general lien
They share equally, in proportion to their amounts
explanation: Real property tax and special assessment liens generally take priority over other liens regardless of when those were recorded. "First recorded wins" does not override tax-lien priority.
citation: NY Real Property Tax Law (tax lien priority)

q: A contractor finishes a kitchen renovation on an owner-occupied single-family house on March 1. Under the NY Lien Law, the notice of mechanic's lien must be filed within:
options: 8 months after completion of the work
30 days after completion of the work
4 months after completion of the work
1 year after completion of the work
explanation: For a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 4 months after the work is completed or the materials are last furnished. The 8-month period applies to other property.

q: A supplier last delivered materials to an office building renovation on January 10. Under the NY Lien Law, the deadline to file a mechanic's lien is generally:
options: 4 months after the final furnishing of materials
8 months after the final furnishing of materials
90 days after the final furnishing of materials
2 years after the final furnishing of materials
explanation: For property other than a single-family dwelling, a mechanic's lien must be filed within 8 months after the final performance of work or final furnishing of materials. The 4-month period is only for single-family dwellings.

q: A buyer's title search reveals a notice of pendency (lis pendens) filed against the property. What does it mean?
options: A final judgment of foreclosure has already been entered against it
The property has unpaid real estate taxes that are now a lien
A neighbor holds a recorded easement over part of the lot
A lawsuit affecting title to or possession of the property is pending
explanation: A notice of pendency warns that litigation affecting the property is pending. Anyone who later acquires an interest takes subject to the outcome. It is a cloud on title, not a judgment or a tax lien.

q: The owner of a rear lot has a recorded right-of-way over the driveway on the front lot. The front lot is sold. What happens to the right-of-way?
options: It continues, and the new owner of the front lot takes subject to it
It ends, because easements are personal to the original parties
It continues only if the new owner signs a new easement agreement
It converts into a revocable license held by the rear owner
explanation: This is an easement appurtenant: the rear lot is the dominant tenement and the front lot is the servient tenement. Appurtenant easements run with the land when either parcel is sold.
citation: NY common law of easements; NY RPL § 291 (recording)

q: An electric utility holds the right to run power lines across a farm. The utility owns no adjoining land. This right is best described as:
options: An easement appurtenant
An easement by necessity
An easement in gross
A license
explanation: An easement in gross benefits a person or entity rather than a neighboring parcel, so there is no dominant tenement. Commercial easements in gross, like utility easements, are interests in land, unlike a revocable license.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (easements)

q: An owner sells the back half of his land, leaving the buyer's parcel with no access to any public road except across the seller's remaining land. What right does the law give the buyer?
options: An easement in gross
An easement by necessity
A license coupled with an interest
An encroachment
explanation: When a parcel is landlocked as a result of dividing commonly owned land, the law implies an easement by necessity across the grantor's remaining land. It lasts as long as the necessity exists.

q: For 11 years, a neighbor has openly and continuously used a path across your land, without permission and without any claim from you. What has the neighbor most likely acquired?
options: Title to the path by adverse possession
A license that you may revoke at any time
An easement in gross
An easement by prescription
explanation: Open, notorious, continuous, and hostile use for 10 years in NY creates a prescriptive easement, which is a right of use, not ownership. Adverse possession requires exclusive possession and transfers title.
citation: NY common law of prescriptive easements (10-year period, CPLR § 212(a))

q: A homeowner verbally tells her neighbor he may fish in her pond whenever he likes. Which statement is true?
options: It is a revocable personal permission, not an interest in land
It is an oral easement appurtenant that runs with the land
It becomes a permanent easement after one year of regular use
It is an easement in gross that the neighbor may sell to others
explanation: A license is personal permission to do something on another's land; it is not an interest in real property. It can generally be revoked and ends on the death of either party or the sale of the land.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (licenses)

q: A survey shows that a neighbor's garage extends two feet onto the buyer's lot. This is an example of:
options: An easement appurtenant
A license
An encroachment
A lis pendens
explanation: An encroachment is an unauthorized intrusion of an improvement onto another's land. It is typically revealed by a survey, not a title search, and it is a common standard exception in title policies.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (encroachments)

q: Local zoning allows two-family houses, but a recorded deed restriction limits a lot to one single-family house. What may the owner build?
options: A two-family house, because zoning overrides private restrictions
Only a single-family house, because the stricter restriction applies
A two-family house, if the owner obtains a building permit
Anything allowed by zoning once the deed is 10 years old
explanation: Private deed restrictions and public zoning both apply, so the owner must satisfy whichever is more restrictive. A building permit does not override a valid private restriction.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (deed restrictions and zoning)

q: In the MARIA test for whether an item is a fixture, the letters stand for:
options: Market value, Age, Removability, Insurability, Appraisal method
Method of payment, Assessment, Rights, Inspection, Agreement
Material used, Attachment, Reasonableness, Improvement, Agreement
Method of annexation, Adaptability, Relationship, Intention, Agreement
explanation: Fixture analysis considers how the item is attached, whether it is adapted to the property, the relationship of the parties, their intention, and any agreement. A specific written agreement or exclusion carries great weight.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

q: A seller installed custom-fitted built-in bookcases and a dining room chandelier. The contract of sale is silent about them. At closing they:
options: Pass to the buyer as fixtures, since the contract does not exclude them
Remain the seller's personal property, which the seller may remove
Pass to the buyer only if they were listed in the property advertisement
May be removed by the seller if they were paid for separately
explanation: Items permanently attached or adapted to the property are presumed fixtures that pass with the real property. A seller who wants to keep one should exclude it in the written contract before signing.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (fixtures)

q: A restaurant tenant bolted commercial ovens to the floor for its business. What are the tenant's rights at the end of the lease?
options: They became the landlord's property when they were bolted down
It may remove them at any time, even years after the lease ends
It may remove them before the lease ends, repairing damage from removal
They must stay unless the landlord pays the tenant for them
explanation: Trade fixtures installed by a commercial tenant for its business remain the tenant's personal property and may be removed by the end of the lease, with any damage repaired. Items left behind may become the landlord's property by accession.
citation: NYS DOS Real Estate Salesperson 77-hr syllabus (trade fixtures)

q: What most clearly distinguishes a freehold estate from a leasehold estate?
options: A freehold can always be passed to heirs by will
A freehold can be created only by a recorded deed
A freehold lasts for an indefinite period of time
A freehold is classified as personal property
explanation: Freehold estates (fee simple and life estates) have no fixed ending date; leaseholds run for a fixed term, a repeating period, or at will. A life estate is a freehold yet cannot be willed by the life tenant, so inheritability is not the test.
citation: General real property law (estates in land)

q: A tenant's interest under a ten-year commercial lease is traditionally classified as:
options: A freehold estate, since the term exceeds one year
A life estate measured by the tenant's business
A fee simple determinable that ends with the lease
A leasehold estate, treated as personal property
explanation: A lease of any length creates a leasehold (nonfreehold) estate, historically called a chattel real and treated as personal property. A long term does not convert it into a freehold.

q: A buyer takes fee simple absolute title to a vacant lot. Which of the following can still limit how the buyer uses it?
options: Nothing, since this fee carries no limits at all
Local zoning and recorded deed restrictions
Only restrictions the buyer personally signed
Only the seller's retained right of re-entry
explanation: Fee simple absolute is the broadest estate, but it remains subject to government powers such as zoning and to private restrictions of record. A seller retains no right of re-entry in an absolute fee; that belongs to a fee on condition subsequent.
citation: General real property law (fee simple absolute)

q: Which deed wording most clearly creates a fee simple determinable?
options: "to the church, but if services stop, grantor may re-enter"
"to the church and its successors and assigns forever"
"to the church for the life of its current pastor"
"to the church for as long as services are held there"
explanation: Durational words such as "so long as," "while," or "until" mark a determinable fee. "But if ... may re-enter" is the language of a fee on condition subsequent, "forever" gives a fee simple absolute, and "for the life of" creates a life estate.

q: The grantor's future interest after a fee simple determinable is called a ____, while the grantor's interest after a fee simple on condition subsequent is a ____.
options: right of re-entry; possibility of reverter
remainder; reversion
reversion; remainder
possibility of reverter; right of re-entry
explanation: A determinable fee is followed by a possibility of reverter, so title returns automatically. A fee on condition subsequent is followed by a right of re-entry (power of termination), which the grantor must exercise. Remainder and reversion follow life estates.

q: An owner deeds a house "to my sister for life" and the deed says nothing more. When the sister dies, who owns the house?
options: The owner or the owner's heirs, by reversion
The sister's heirs, as remaindermen
The State of New York, by escheat
The sister's executor, by survivorship
explanation: When no remainderman is named, the future interest stays with the grantor as a reversion and returns to the grantor or the grantor's heirs. The sister held only a life estate, so she had nothing to pass to her heirs.

q: Grace holds a life estate measured by her own life and sells it to Hal. Grace later dies while Hal is still alive. What happens to Hal's interest?
options: It continues for the rest of Hal's life
Hal now owns fee simple since he paid value
It passes to Hal's heirs when Hal dies
It ends, and the remainderman or reversioner takes
explanation: A life tenant can transfer only what she holds. Hal bought an estate measured by Grace's life (pur autre vie), so it ends at Grace's death. The trap is assuming the buyer's own life becomes the measuring life.

q: Without the remainderman's consent, a life tenant tears down a sound barn and clear-cuts the woodlot for timber. The remainderman's best claim is for:
options: Partition
Adverse possession
Waste
Breach of seisin
explanation: A life tenant must not damage or deplete the property in a way that harms the future interest; destroying a sound building and stripping timber is waste. Partition divides co-owned property and does not apply between a life tenant and a remainderman.
citation: General real property law (waste); RPAPL Article 8 (actions for waste)

q: A life tenant lets the roof leak for years and makes no ordinary repairs, and the framing rots. This is best described as:
options: Permissive waste
Voluntary waste
Constructive eviction
Functional obsolescence
explanation: Waste by neglect, such as failing to make ordinary repairs, is permissive waste. Voluntary (affirmative) waste is a deliberate harmful act, like demolishing a building.

q: Absent any restriction in the granting deed, which action may a life tenant take without the remainderman's consent?
options: Sell the property in fee simple to a buyer
Lease the property for the duration of the life estate
Demolish the house to build a larger one
Leave the property to a friend by will
explanation: A life tenant may possess, lease, mortgage, or sell the life estate itself, but any lease ends when the measuring life ends. She cannot convey a fee she does not own, commit waste, or will away an interest that ends at death.

q: While a life estate is in effect, who is ordinarily responsible for paying the real property taxes?
options: The life tenant
The remainderman
The original grantor
Both, in equal shares
explanation: The life tenant has possession and the income from the property, so ordinary carrying costs such as property taxes and routine repairs fall on the life tenant. The remainderman has no current possession.
citation: General real property law (life tenant duties)

q: An owner deeds a cottage "to Ira for as long as Ira's mother lives." Ira holds:
options: A life estate measured by Ira's life
An estate for years
A fee simple determinable
A life estate pur autre vie
explanation: An estate measured by the life of someone other than the holder (here, Ira's mother) is a life estate pur autre vie. "For as long as" sounds determinable, but an estate that must end at a person's death is a life estate, not a fee.

q: While a life estate is in effect, the remainderman:
options: May share occupancy with the life tenant
Owns a future interest that may be sold now
Has no property interest of any kind yet
Must pay the property taxes each year
explanation: A remainderman has a present ownership of a future interest, which can be sold or mortgaged, but no right to possession until the life estate ends. Possession and ordinary carrying costs belong to the life tenant.

q: A widow asks whether she has a dower right in a house her late husband owned in his own name in New York. The correct response is that:
options: Dower gives her a life estate in one-third
Dower is abolished; she may have a right of election
Dower applies only to the marital residence
Dower applies if she claims it within six months
explanation: New York abolished dower and curtesy. A surviving spouse is protected instead by the statutory right of election against the deceased spouse's will. The one-third life estate describes historic common-law dower.

q: Which of the following is NOT available to a married couple or a surviving spouse in New York today?
options: Curtesy
Tenancy by the entirety
Right of election
Joint tenancy
explanation: Curtesy, the historic life estate of a husband in his deceased wife's land, has been abolished in New York along with dower. Married couples may hold title as tenants by the entirety or joint tenants, and a surviving spouse has a right of election.

q: New York's homestead exemption primarily:
options: Gives a surviving spouse a life estate in the home
Lowers school taxes on owner-occupied homes
Bars any foreclosure of a primary residence
Shields some home equity from judgment creditors
explanation: The homestead exemption protects a limited amount of equity in a principal residence from being taken to satisfy money judgments. It is not a surviving-spouse life estate (New York does not recognize one) and is not the STAR school tax program.

q: A homeowner defaults on a mortgage he signed when buying his primary residence. Does the homestead exemption prevent the lender's foreclosure?
options: Yes; a primary residence can never be foreclosed
No; it does not defeat a mortgage he gave voluntarily
Yes, if he has lived there for at least ten years
No, because it covers only vacant investment land
explanation: The exemption limits what unsecured money-judgment creditors can reach; it does not cancel a lien the owner voluntarily granted as security for the purchase loan. It applies to a principal residence, not vacant land.

q: A tenant signs a lease running from March 1 to August 31 of the same year. This lease creates:
options: A periodic tenancy
An estate for years
A tenancy at will
A tenancy at sufferance
explanation: Any lease with a definite beginning and ending date is an estate for years, even when the term is shorter than a year. A periodic tenancy has no fixed end and renews period to period.

q: Which of the following estates ends upon the death of either the landlord or the tenant?
options: A tenancy at will
An estate for years
A month-to-month tenancy
A fee simple absolute
explanation: A tenancy at will rests on the parties' continuing consent, so it ends when either party dies. An estate for years and a periodic tenancy survive the death of either party and bind the estate.
citation: General real property law (tenancy at will)

q: What separates a tenant at sufferance from a trespasser?
options: The tenant at sufferance first entered lawfully
The tenant at sufferance has a written lease
The tenant at sufferance owes no rent at all
The tenant at sufferance has the owner's consent
explanation: A tenant at sufferance came into possession under a valid tenancy and stayed after it ended without the owner's consent. A trespasser never had a right to enter. Continuing consent would make it a tenancy at will, not sufferance.

q: A tenant's one-year lease expires, the tenant stays, and the landlord accepts the next monthly rent payment. Absent another agreement, New York law generally treats the tenancy as:
options: A renewal for another full year
A tenancy at sufferance
A month-to-month tenancy
A tenancy at will with no notice
explanation: New York does not apply the common-law rule that accepting rent renews the lease for a full term; a holdover whose rent is accepted is generally a month-to-month tenant. Acceptance of rent shows consent, so it is no longer sufferance.

q: An owner lets her nephew live in a spare house with no set term and no fixed rental period, until either of them decides to end it. This is:
options: An estate for years
A tenancy at will
A tenancy at sufferance
A life estate
explanation: Possession with the owner's consent but no fixed term or period is a tenancy at will. Sufferance requires a holdover without consent, and an estate for years needs a definite term.

q: A deed conveys land "to Ana and Ben," who are not married to each other, with no other language. Under New York law they hold title as:
options: Joint tenants
Tenants by the entirety
Tenants in common
Owners in severalty
explanation: New York presumes a tenancy in common when real property goes to two or more persons unless the instrument expressly declares a joint tenancy. Naming two grantees alone does not create survivorship.

q: A deed conveys a house "to Carla and Dev," who are married to each other, and says nothing about the form of ownership. They hold title as:
options: Tenants in common
Tenants by the entirety
Joint tenants
Owners in severalty
explanation: A disposition to persons married to each other creates a tenancy by the entirety unless the instrument expressly declares a tenancy in common or joint tenancy. The tenancy-in-common default applies only to unmarried co-grantees.

q: Three unrelated friends own a cabin as joint tenants with right of survivorship. One dies, leaving a will that gives everything to her son. Who owns the cabin?
options: The son and both friends, one-third each
The son alone, under the terms of the will
The two surviving friends, one-half each
The friends and the son as tenants in common
explanation: Survivorship operates at the moment of death, so the deceased joint tenant's interest passes to the surviving joint tenants and never enters her estate. A will cannot override it: 1 ÷ 2 survivors gives each one-half.

q: Eva, Finn, and Gia own land as joint tenants. Eva sells her interest to Hugo. Later Finn dies. Who owns the land, and how?
options: Gia two-thirds and Hugo one-third, as tenants in common
Gia and Hugo one-half each, as joint tenants
Gia owns all of it by right of survivorship
Gia, Hugo, and Finn's heirs one-third each
explanation: Eva's sale severed her one-third, so Hugo holds 1/3 as a tenant in common; Finn and Gia stayed joint tenants as to the other 2/3. When Finn died, Gia took his share by survivorship: 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 for Gia, with Hugo still holding 1/3.
citation: General real property law (severance of joint tenancy)

q: The four unities traditionally required to create a joint tenancy are:
options: Possession, interest, time, and marriage
Possession, consent, title, and recording
Possession, interest, time, and title
Interest, title, survival, and severalty
explanation: Joint tenants must take equal interests (interest), by the same deed (title), at the same time (time), with equal rights to possess the whole (possession). Marriage is the added fifth unity for a tenancy by the entirety.

q: Two investors take title to a building as tenants in common, and one paid 70% of the price. Which statement is true?
options: The law requires them to hold equal half shares
The larger investor alone may occupy the building
Each one's share passes to the other at death
Their shares may be unequal, such as 70% and 30%
explanation: Tenants in common may hold unequal undivided shares, but each has the right to possess the whole property. Unequal shares are a key contrast with joint tenancy, and there is no survivorship among tenants in common.
citation: General real property law (tenancy in common)

q: A tenancy by the entirety requires the four unities of a joint tenancy plus:
options: A valid marriage between the owners
A recorded survivorship affidavit
Equal financial contributions
Use as the couple's primary home
explanation: Tenancy by the entirety is available only to spouses, so marriage is the fifth unity. It does not depend on who paid what or on the property being the couple's residence.

q: A married couple owns their home as tenants by the entirety and later divorces. Absent an agreement or court order, they then generally own it as:
options: Joint tenants with survivorship
Tenants by the entirety until death
The higher earner, in severalty
Tenants in common
explanation: Divorce ends the marriage that a tenancy by the entirety requires, and in New York the former spouses generally become tenants in common, with no survivorship. Title does not pass automatically to either spouse alone.
citation: Stelz v. Shreck, 128 N.Y. 263 (1891); general real property law (tenancy by the entirety)

q: A wife holds her home with her husband as tenants by the entirety. She wants to sell over his objection. Which statement is correct?
options: She may sell the whole house since she paid most of it
She cannot convey the whole or force a partition alone
She may force a partition sale as any co-owner can
She may end the survivorship by deeding to herself
explanation: A tenancy by the entirety protects each spouse's survivorship right; one spouse cannot unilaterally convey the entire property or compel partition while the marriage lasts. Who paid more does not change that.
citation: General real property law (tenancy by the entirety)

q: Two tenants in common cannot agree whether to sell their jointly owned lot. Either of them may ask a court to:
options: Declare a reversion to the grantor
Convert it to a tenancy by the entirety
Grant one owner an easement by necessity
Order a partition by division or sale
explanation: A partition action lets a co-owner end the co-ownership: the court divides the land physically or, if that is impractical, orders a sale and divides the proceeds.

q: A corporation with 500 shareholders takes title to a warehouse. How is the warehouse owned?
options: As tenants in common among the shareholders
As joint tenants among the board members
In severalty, by the corporation as one entity
In common by the officers who signed the deed
explanation: A corporation is a single legal person, so property titled in its name is owned in severalty. Shareholders own stock in the corporation, not undivided interests in its real estate.
citation: General real property law (ownership by entities)

q: Investors want to own a rental building with personal protection from the business's debts while managing it themselves. The form most often chosen is:
options: A general partnership
A joint tenancy
A tenancy in common
A limited liability company
explanation: An LLC lets members participate in management while generally shielding their personal assets from the company's debts. General partners, joint tenants, and tenants in common have no such entity shield.

q: When real estate is placed in a trust, legal title is held by the:
options: Beneficiary
Trustor
Trustee
Executor
explanation: The trustor (settlor) creates the trust; the trustee holds legal title and manages under the trust instrument; the beneficiary receives the benefits (equitable interest). An executor administers a decedent's estate, not a trust.

q: Several investors join together to buy, build, and sell one specific subdivision, then disband. This arrangement is best described as:
options: A real estate investment trust
A tenancy by the entirety
A joint venture
A housing cooperative
explanation: A joint venture combines parties for a single project of limited duration. A REIT is an ongoing investment vehicle owning many properties, and a tenancy by the entirety is available only to spouses.

q: An owner signs a five-year lease of her building. Which right in her bundle of rights does she temporarily transfer to the tenant?
options: Disposition
Possession
Legal title
Escheat
explanation: A lease transfers possession (and use) for the term while the owner keeps title and the right of disposition, meaning she can still sell the building subject to the lease. Escheat is a government power, not an owner's right.
citation: General real property law (bundle of rights)

q: Which of the following is NOT part of a private owner's traditional bundle of rights?
options: Right of exclusion
Right of escheat
Right of enjoyment
Right of disposition
explanation: The bundle includes possession, control, enjoyment, exclusion, and disposition. Escheat is a government power under which property passes to the state when an owner dies with no will and no heirs.
citation: General real property law (bundle of rights)

q: A homeowner cuts down a tree in the yard and stacks the logs for firewood. The logs are now:
options: Personal property, since they were severed
Real property, since they grew on the land
Fixtures, since they remain on the parcel
Trade fixtures belonging to the homeowner
explanation: A growing tree is part of the real property, but severance converts it into personal property (chattel). Logs merely lying on the ground are not attached, so they are not fixtures.
citation: General real property law (real vs. personal property)

q: A tenant farmer plants an annual crop, but the lease ends without the tenant's fault before harvest. The doctrine that may allow the tenant to come back and harvest is:
options: Accretion
Severalty
Escheat
Emblements
explanation: Emblements are annual crops produced by labor; a tenant whose tenancy ends through no fault of their own before harvest may generally enter to harvest them. Accretion concerns soil deposited by water.

q: A railroad sells a developer the right to build an office tower over its tracks while keeping the tracks in use. The developer has acquired:
options: Air rights
Riparian rights
Subsurface rights
An easement by necessity
explanation: Air rights, the right to use the space above the surface, can be sold separately from the land. Subsurface rights concern the area below the surface, and riparian rights concern flowing water.

q: An owner sells farmland but keeps the right to extract the natural gas beneath it. The owner has:
options: Created a tenancy in common with the buyer
Retained the littoral rights to the land
Reserved the subsurface (mineral) rights
Kept a life estate in the surface only
explanation: Surface and subsurface rights can be separated; reserving the gas leaves the seller with mineral rights while the buyer owns the surface. Littoral rights concern land bordering lakes or seas.

q: A house sits on the shore of Lake George. The owner's rights to access and use the lake water are called:
options: Littoral rights
Riparian rights
Percolating rights
Avulsion rights
explanation: Littoral rights belong to owners of land bordering stationary bodies of water such as lakes and seas. Riparian rights belong to owners bordering flowing water such as rivers and streams.

q: A spring flood suddenly cuts a new channel for a stream, abruptly tearing away part of a farm. This sudden change is called:
options: Accretion
Reliction
Avulsion
Alluvion
explanation: Avulsion is a sudden, perceptible loss or shift of land caused by water. Accretion is the gradual buildup of soil (the deposit itself is alluvion), and reliction is land exposed as water gradually recedes.
citation: General real property law (water-related land changes)

q: A village levies a charge against a home to pay for new sidewalks along its frontage. If unpaid, the resulting lien is best classified as:
options: Voluntary and general
Involuntary and specific
Voluntary and specific
Involuntary and general
explanation: A special assessment lien arises by law without the owner's consent (involuntary) and attaches only to the benefited parcel (specific). Calling it general confuses it with a judgment or federal tax lien, which reach all of a debtor's property.
citation: General real property law (special assessment liens)

q: The IRS files a notice of federal tax lien against a taxpayer who owes unpaid income tax. How is this lien classified?
options: Voluntary and general
Voluntary and specific
Involuntary and specific
Involuntary and general
explanation: A federal tax lien arises by operation of law (involuntary) and attaches to all of the taxpayer's property and rights to property (general). The trap is treating it like a property tax lien, which is specific to one parcel.

q: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between liens and encumbrances?
options: Every encumbrance is a lien, but only some liens are encumbrances
Liens and encumbrances are two names for the same interest
Every lien is an encumbrance, but some encumbrances are not liens
An encumbrance must be recorded, while a lien never needs recording
explanation: An encumbrance is any interest that burdens title or use; a lien is the money-claim type of encumbrance. Easements, restrictions and encroachments are encumbrances that secure no debt, so not every encumbrance is a lien.

q: A homeowner borrows against her house and signs a home equity mortgage. This lien is:
options: Involuntary, because the bank can foreclose without her consent
General, because it reaches all property she owns
Statutory, because the Lien Law creates it on signing
Voluntary and specific, attaching only to the mortgaged parcel
explanation: The owner chooses to give the mortgage (voluntary), and it secures the debt only with the described property (specific). The foreclosure remedy does not make the lien involuntary; how a lien is created decides that label.

q: A plumber files a notice of mechanic's lien against a client's building. Under the NY Lien Law, when must the plumber serve a copy of the notice on the owner?
options: Within 4 months after filing the notice
Within 10 days after the last day of work
At least 30 days before filing the notice
Within 5 days before or 30 days after filing
explanation: Lien Law §11 requires service on the owner within 5 days before or 30 days after the notice of lien is filed. The 4-month figure is the filing deadline for a single-family dwelling, not the service window.

q: A contractor files a notice of lien and serves the owner properly, but never files proof of service with the county clerk. What is the result after 35 days from filing?
options: The lien stays valid but cannot be foreclosed until proof is filed
The notice terminates as a lien
The lien converts into a general lien on the owner's property
The owner must post a bond to keep the lien from expanding
explanation: Lien Law §11 says failure to file proof of service within 35 days after the notice of lien is filed terminates the notice as a lien. Proper service alone is not enough; the filing of proof is what preserves it.

q: A notice of mechanic's lien was filed on May 12, 2026, against an office building. If the lienor does nothing further, when does it stop being a lien?
options: November 12, 2026, six months after filing
January 12, 2027, eight months after filing
May 12, 2027, one year after filing
May 12, 2036, ten years after filing
explanation: Lien Law §17 limits a mechanic's lien to one year after filing unless a foreclosure action with a notice of pendency is filed or the lien is extended. Ten years is the judgment-lien period, and eight months is a filing deadline, not a duration.

q: A contractor's lien on a single-family house will expire in three weeks. The contractor is not ready to sue to foreclose. How can the lien be extended?
options: Only by an order of a court of record
By filing an extension with the county clerk
By re-serving the owner with a new notice
By recording a second notice of lien
explanation: Lien Law §17 bars extension by simple filing for a lien on a single-family dwelling; it may only be extended by court order. For other property, filing an extension with the county clerk within the first year is allowed.

q: A supplier holds a mechanic's lien on a 20-unit apartment building. Before the first year runs out, the supplier files an extension with the county clerk. For how long does that filed extension continue the lien?
options: Six months from the original expiration
No more than one year from its filing
Until the building is sold or refinanced
Ten years, like a docketed judgment
explanation: Under Lien Law §17, a filed extension cannot continue the lien for more than one year from the extension's filing; after that, a foreclosure action or a court order is needed. Liens do not ride along until a sale, and the 10-year period belongs to judgments.

q: An owner wants to sell a building that has a $23,600 mechanic's lien on it. To discharge the lien by bond under the Lien Law, the bond must be at least:
explanation: Lien Law §19(4) requires a bond equal to 110% of the lien: $23,600 × 1.10 = $25,960. $23,600 omits the 10% cushion, $27,140 uses 115%, and $35,400 uses 150%.

q: An owner posts a proper bond and obtains discharge of a mechanic's lien. What is the effect?
options: The lienor loses all right to be paid for the work
The lien is moved to the owner's other real estate
The lien stays on title until the claim is resolved
The claim shifts to the bond and the land is freed
explanation: Discharging a lien by bond releases the real property; the lienor's claim is now secured by the bond instead. The lienor does not lose its claim; it simply must pursue the bond rather than the land.

q: A contractor finishes renovating an owner-occupied two-family house on February 2. What is the deadline to file a notice of mechanic's lien?
options: 8 months after completion, since it is not a single-family dwelling
4 months after completion, since the owner lives in the house
90 days after completion, the same as any residential job
1 year after completion, the life of a mechanic's lien
explanation: Lien Law §10's shorter 4-month window applies only to a single-family dwelling; a two-family house falls under the general 8-month deadline. Owner occupancy does not trigger the 4-month rule, and one year is how long a filed lien lasts.

q: A contractor starts work on January 5. A bank records a mortgage on the property on February 1. The unpaid contractor files a notice of lien on April 2. Under NY law, which has priority?
options: The lien, because it relates back to the January 5 start of work
The mortgage, because it was recorded before the notice was filed
The lien, because mechanic's liens always outrank mortgages
Neither, because the two share any foreclosure proceeds equally
explanation: Lien Law §13 gives a mechanic's lien priority over interests not recorded when the notice of lien is filed; a mortgage recorded earlier stays ahead. NY measures from the filing of the notice, not the start of work, which is the relation-back trap from other states.

q: An owner's renovation contract with a general contractor is $40,000. The job is complete and the owner has paid $34,000 in good faith. An unpaid subcontractor then files a $10,000 lien. What is the most the lien can recover against the owner's property?
explanation: Under Lien Law §4, a subcontractor's lien cannot exceed the amount earned and unpaid on the owner's contract when the notice is filed: $40,000 − $34,000 = $6,000. The full $10,000 claim ignores this cap, and $4,000 wrongly subtracts $6,000 from $10,000.

q: A home improvement contract includes a clause, signed before any work begins, in which the contractor gives up any right to file a mechanic's lien. This clause is:
options: Void as against public policy
Enforceable if the owner paid a deposit
Valid only if it is notarized and recorded
Binding on subcontractors but not the contractor
explanation: Lien Law §34 voids any agreement waiving the right to file or enforce a mechanic's lien. The statute does allow a written waiver delivered at or after payment for the work, but an advance waiver in the contract is unenforceable.

q: A contractor who is owed $8,000 knowingly files a notice of lien claiming $19,000. If a court finds the amount was willfully exaggerated, the likely result is that:
options: The lien is reduced to $8,000 and stays in force
The lien remains valid until the owner posts a bond
The lien is void and the contractor may owe damages
The contractor must refile within 30 days at $8,000
explanation: Under Lien Law §§39 and 39-a, a willfully exaggerated lien is void, and the lienor can be liable for damages, including the cost of discharging it. A court does not simply trim the amount when the exaggeration was willful.

q: A retail tenant hires a contractor to install new storefront lighting. The landlord did not request or consent to the work. If the tenant does not pay, the contractor's lien can attach to:
options: The landlord's fee title to the building
The tenant's leasehold interest only
The landlord's other properties in the county
Nothing, because tenants cannot contract for work
explanation: A tenant is an "owner" of its leasehold under Lien Law §2, and §3 gives a lien on an owner's interest for work done with that owner's consent or at its request. Without the landlord's affirmative consent, the lien reaches only the tenant's leasehold, not the landlord's fee.

q: A judgment against Ruth was docketed in Albany County in 2023. In 2025, she buys a house in Albany County. What is the status of the house?
options: The judgment is a lien on the house
The house is exempt because it was bought later
A new lawsuit is needed to reach the house
The lien attaches only if Ruth agrees in writing
explanation: A docketed judgment is a general lien on the debtor's real property in that county, including property acquired later during the 10-year lien period. No new suit or consent is needed for the lien to attach.

q: A creditor's judgment is docketed in Westchester County, but the debtor also owns a cabin in Ulster County. How can the creditor obtain a lien on the cabin?
options: Record a lis pendens against the debtor's home
File a mechanic's lien in Ulster County
Wait; a docketed judgment reaches every county
Docket a transcript of the judgment in Ulster County
explanation: A judgment is a lien only on real property in a county where it is docketed, so the creditor must docket it with the Ulster County clerk. A judgment does not automatically reach every county, and a lis pendens does not create a money lien.

q: A notice of pendency (lis pendens) is filed against a property. Under the CPLR, how long does it remain effective?
options: 1 year, renewable by filing an extension
10 years, like a docketed money judgment
Until the property is sold to a new owner
3 years, extendable by court order for good cause
explanation: CPLR §6513 makes a notice of pendency effective for 3 years from filing, and a court may extend it for a like period on a showing of good cause. One year is the mechanic's lien period and 10 years is the judgment-lien period.

q: A buyer closes on a lot one month after a neighbor filed a notice of pendency in a boundary lawsuit against the seller. The buyer never searched title. How is the buyer affected?
options: The buyer is bound by the outcome of the lawsuit
The buyer takes free because he lacked actual notice
The suit is dismissed because the owner has changed
The seller alone bears the risk of the suit's result
explanation: A filed notice of pendency is constructive notice, so a later purchaser is bound by the judgment as if a party to the suit. Lack of actual knowledge does not protect a buyer who could have found the filing in a title search.

q: Before trial, a court orders a defendant's real property held so that it will be available if the plaintiff later wins a money judgment. This is called:
options: A writ of execution
An attachment
A lis pendens
A satisfaction
explanation: An attachment is a prejudgment remedy that seizes or holds property to secure a possible judgment. A writ of execution comes after judgment to enforce it, and a lis pendens only gives notice of a suit affecting title.

q: A notice of federal tax lien was filed against an owner in 2023. In 2026, the owner fails to pay the year's real property taxes. Which lien generally has priority against the house?
options: The federal tax lien, because federal claims always come first
The federal tax lien, because its notice was filed earlier
Neither; they share proceeds in proportion to the amounts
The real property tax lien, despite being later in time
explanation: Federal law yields to local real property tax and special assessment liens that have priority under local law, even when the federal notice was filed first. The trap is assuming either federal status or first-in-time filing beats the property tax lien.

q: A bank's mortgage was recorded in 2020. In 2024, the IRS files a notice of federal tax lien against the homeowner. Which interest generally has priority on the house?
options: The bank's mortgage, recorded before the tax lien notice
The federal tax lien, because it is a government claim
The federal tax lien, because it is a general lien
Whichever creditor first starts a foreclosure action
explanation: A federal tax lien is not valid against a holder of a security interest, such as a mortgagee, until the notice of federal tax lien is filed, so the earlier mortgage stays ahead. Unlike local real property taxes, a federal tax lien gets no special priority over prior recorded mortgages.

q: Lot A's owner holds a recorded easement to use a driveway that crosses Lot B to reach the street. Which statement is correct?
options: Lot B is the dominant estate
Lot A is the servient estate
Lot B is the servient estate
Neither lot is dominant or servient
explanation: The servient estate bears the burden of the easement; Lot B's land is crossed, so it is servient. Lot A benefits from the easement, which makes it the dominant estate.

q: An owner sells the front half of her land but, in the deed to the buyer, keeps for herself the right to keep crossing the front half to reach her well. Her right was created by:
options: Reservation in the deed
Prescription
Implication from necessity
An oral license
explanation: When a grantor conveys land but keeps an easement over it for her own use, the easement is created by reservation. Prescription requires years of adverse use, and a license is a revocable permission, not an interest in land.

q: A single owner's two lots were served by an underground sewer line running from the rear house across the front lot, with a visible cleanout cap. He sells the front lot without mentioning the line. The rear lot most likely has:
options: An easement in gross held by the sewer district
No right, because the deed did not mention the line
A license that the new front-lot owner may revoke
An implied easement based on the prior use
explanation: When one owner's land is divided, an apparent, continuous use that is necessary for the retained parcel's enjoyment can create an easement by implication. The deed's silence does not defeat it, and the rear lot's right is appurtenant, not in gross.
citation: General real property law (easements by implication)

q: A landlocked parcel received an easement by necessity across a neighbor's land. Years later, the county builds a public road along the parcel's back line. What is the likely effect?
options: The easement continues permanently because it was recorded
The easement ends because the necessity has ended
The easement becomes an easement in gross for the county
The neighbor must now pay for the parcel's road frontage
explanation: An easement by necessity lasts only as long as the necessity that created it; once the parcel has its own public access, the easement ends. An express easement by grant would not end this way.
citation: General real property law (easements by necessity)

q: The owner of a dominant parcel buys the servient parcel that his driveway easement crosses. What happens to the easement?
options: It is extinguished by merger
It becomes a license he may revoke
It continues as a separate right
It converts to an easement in gross
explanation: An easement is a right in another's land. When one person owns both the dominant and the servient parcels, the easement ends by merger, and it does not revive merely if the parcels are later separated.
citation: General real property law (termination of easements)

q: A recorded right-of-way created by deed has not been used for 15 years, but its owner has done nothing else to show an intent to give it up. Under NY law, the easement:
options: Ended automatically after 10 years of nonuse
Became a license that either party may revoke
Is still in effect, because nonuse alone does not end it
Passed by prescription to the servient owner
explanation: An easement created by grant is not lost by nonuse alone; abandonment requires an intent to abandon shown by clear acts. The 10-year figure is the adverse possession period, which requires adverse acts by the servient owner, not just nonuse.
citation: General real property law (abandonment of easements)

q: A dominant owner no longer needs a utility path across a neighbor's yard and wants to end the easement permanently. The cleanest way is to:
options: Stop using the path for one full year
Give the neighbor a written release and record it
Tell the neighbor orally that the path is no longer needed
Let the neighbor build a fence across the path
explanation: A written release from the dominant owner to the servient owner, recorded, terminates the easement and clears the record. Oral statements and brief nonuse do not reliably end a recorded easement.
citation: General real property law (termination of easements)

q: What is the key difference between an easement by prescription and title by adverse possession?
options: Prescription requires 20 years, adverse possession 10
Adverse possession needs no hostile use; prescription does
Prescription gives title, adverse possession only use
Prescription gives a right to use; adverse possession gives title
explanation: Both require open, notorious, continuous and hostile use for the 10-year statutory period in NY, but prescription yields only an easement, while adverse possession transfers ownership.

q: For 12 years a neighbor has walked across Dan's yard to reach a lake. When the use began, the neighbor asked Dan, who said, "Sure, go ahead." Does the neighbor have a prescriptive easement?
options: No, because the use was permissive rather than hostile
Yes, because the use lasted more than 10 years
Yes, because Dan never revoked the permission
No, because a path to a lake cannot be an easement
explanation: Prescription requires hostile use, meaning use without the owner's permission. Use that began with permission is a license, and the passage of time alone does not convert it into an easement.

q: A homeowner lets her neighbor park a boat in her side yard, with no written agreement. She then sells the house. What is the neighbor's right to keep parking there?
options: It continues because it is an easement appurtenant
It continues for 10 years from when it began
It ends, because the license does not bind the buyer
It ends only after the buyer gives 30 days' notice
explanation: Informal permission to use land is a license: a personal, generally revocable privilege, not an interest in land. A license ends when the licensor sells the property or revokes it, so the buyer is not bound.

q: A landowner grants a gravel company the right to enter her land and remove sand and gravel. This right is best described as:
options: A license
An easement appurtenant
A profit (profit à prendre)
An encroachment
explanation: A profit is the right to enter another's land and take something from it, such as gravel, timber or minerals. A plain easement allows use but not removal of resources, and a license is a revocable permission rather than an interest in land.

q: A subdivision's recorded declaration bars detached garages. A new owner starts building one. A neighbor who owns a lot bound by the same declaration most likely may:
options: Do nothing, since only the town enforces such limits
Ask the building inspector to revoke the owner's deed
Seek a court injunction to stop the construction
Reclaim the lot under a possibility of reverter
explanation: Restrictive covenants under a common subdivision plan run with the land and may be enforced by other benefited lot owners, usually by injunction. Private deed restrictions are separate from zoning, and a covenant breach does not cause a reversion of title.

q: A 1940s deed in a buyer's chain of title contains a covenant barring sale to members of a certain race. Today this covenant is:
options: Enforceable only against buyers who knew of it
Unenforceable under fair housing law
Binding until removed by a vote of neighbors
Valid if no one has challenged it in 50 years
explanation: Racially restrictive covenants cannot be enforced by courts and violate federal and state fair housing laws. They remain void regardless of buyer knowledge, neighbor votes, or how long they sat unchallenged.
citation: Shelley v. Kraemer (1948); Fair Housing Act, 42 U.S.C. §3604

q: A neighbor's hedge has grown two feet over the property line for 14 years. The neighbor now claims the strip by adverse possession. Under NY law, the hedge encroachment is:
options: Enough for title, since 10 years have passed
Enough only if the neighbor also paid the taxes
Deemed permissive and not adverse
Converted into an easement by prescription
explanation: RPAPL §543 deems de minimis non-structural encroachments, such as fences, hedges, plantings and sheds, permissive and non-adverse. Without hostility, the 10-year period does not ripen into title or a prescriptive easement.

q: Custom-cut storm windows made for a house are stored in the basement when the sale closes. The contract is silent. How are they most likely treated?
options: As the seller's personal property because they are unattached
As fixtures that convey, since they were adapted to the house
As the seller's property unless the buyer pays separately
As trade fixtures the seller may remove within 30 days
explanation: Under the adaptation factor, items made specifically for a particular building are generally treated as fixtures even when temporarily detached. Physical attachment is only one factor; intention shown by adaptation controls here.

q: A tenant and an owner each mount an identical wall air-conditioner. Which fixture factor most explains why the tenant's unit is more likely to remain personal property?
options: The relationship of the parties
The method of annexation
The adaptability of the item
The cost of the item
explanation: Courts presume a tenant installs items for its own use and intends to remove them, while an owner's improvements are presumed permanent. The attachment method is identical here, so the parties' relationship is the deciding factor.

q: A seller's dining room chandelier is wired into the ceiling. The signed contract states, "Seller excludes the dining room chandelier." At closing, the chandelier:
options: Must stay, because it is wired in as a fixture
Belongs to the buyer unless a bill of sale is signed
Must stay unless the seller installs a substitute
May be removed by the seller under the agreement
explanation: A written agreement between the parties overrides the other fixture tests. Even a firmly attached item may be excluded, though the seller should leave the wiring safely capped.

q: A bakery tenant's lease expires and the tenant moves out, leaving its bolted-down display cases and ovens. No lease clause addresses them. Who generally owns them now?
options: The tenant, who may return to remove them at any time
The tenant, until the landlord pays their fair value
The landlord, by accession
The next tenant of the space
explanation: Trade fixtures remain the tenant's personal property only if removed by the end of the tenancy; items left behind generally become the landlord's property by accession. The tenant has no open-ended right to return for them.

q: A life tenant plants a field of corn in May and dies in July, before the harvest. Who is generally entitled to harvest the crop?
options: The life tenant's estate
The remainderman alone
The county where the land lies
Whoever first cuts the crop
explanation: Under the doctrine of emblements, a tenant whose estate ends unexpectedly through no fault of its own, such as the end of a measuring life, may enter to harvest annual crops it planted. The remainderman takes the land but not that crop.

q: Which is generally treated as personal property rather than part of the real estate?
options: An apple orchard
A planted wheat crop
A stand of oak trees
Perennial shrubbery
explanation: Annual crops produced by labor (fructus industriales), such as wheat, are generally treated as personal property. Trees, orchards and perennial plantings (fructus naturales) are part of the real property.
